title: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA)
remediation_guide: Your API is returning data for ANY user ID passed in the URL, not just the logged-in user. Fix: In your route handler, compare the requested :id against the authenticated user's ID from the JWT token. If they don't match (and the user isn't an admin), return a 403 Forbidden response immediately. Never trust user-supplied IDs without authorization checks.

title: SQL Injection via Search Parameter
remediation_guide: Your search endpoint is directly concatenating user input into a database query. An attacker can type ' OR '1'='1 and read your entire database. Fix: Use parameterized queries or prepared statements. If you're using Node.js with Knex, replace db.raw(`SELECT * FROM items WHERE name = '${q}'`) with db('items').where('name', q). Never build SQL strings with user input.

title: JWT Secret Hardcoded in Source Code
remediation_guide: A JWT signing secret was found hardcoded in your auth.js file (value: 'mysecretkey123'). Anyone who reads your codebase — including anyone with GitHub access — can forge valid login tokens. Fix: Move the secret to an environment variable: process.env.JWT_SECRET. Use a tool like dotenv locally, and set it as a secure environment variable in production (AWS Secrets Manager, Vercel env vars, etc.). Rotate the old secret immediately.

title: Missing Rate Limiting on Auth Endpoint
remediation_guide: Your login endpoint has no rate limiting. An attacker can try thousands of username/password combinations per minute (brute-force attack). Fix: Install the express-rate-limit package. Add this middleware to your login route: const limiter = rateLimit({ windowMs: 15 * 60 * 1000, max: 10, message: 'Too many login attempts' }). This allows only 10 attempts per 15 minutes per IP address.

title: Sensitive Data Exposed in API Response
remediation_guide: Your user profile API is returning the full database row, including hashed passwords, internal IDs, and admin flags. Even hashed passwords should never leave your server. Fix: Create an explicit response object that only includes the fields a client needs (e.g., { id, name, email, avatar_url }). Never use SELECT * and never return the full ORM object directly. A simple pattern: const safeUser = { id: user.id, name: user.name, email: user.email }; res.json(safeUser);

title: Dependency with Known RCE Vulnerability
remediation_guide: Your project uses lodash version 4.17.15 which has a known Prototype Pollution vulnerability (CVE-2019-10744) that can lead to Remote Code Execution. Fix: Update lodash immediately by running: npm update lodash. After updating, run npm audit to verify no other vulnerable packages remain. Set up a scheduled npm audit check in your CI/CD pipeline to catch this automatically in the future.

title: Missing Security Headers
remediation_guide: Your API responses are missing critical HTTP security headers (Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options). Without these, your app is vulnerable to clickjacking and MIME-sniffing attacks. Fix: Install the 'helmet' package (npm install helmet) and add app.use(helmet()) near the top of your Express server file, before any route definitions. This one line adds all critical security headers automatically.

title: Verbose Error Messages Leaking Stack Traces
remediation_guide: When your server crashes, it's returning the full Node.js stack trace to the browser including file paths, line numbers, and internal variable names. This gives attackers a map of your codebase. Fix: Create a global error handler in Express and ensure NODE_ENV is set to 'production' in deployment. In production mode, return only a generic error message: res.status(500).json({ error: 'An internal error occurred' }). Log the full error server-side only.
